title: Can Canada claw its way back into the Chinese lobster market?
summary: The Canadian lobster industry is thinking of ways to recapture the Chinese market after competitors took advantage of retaliatory tariffs. Vietnam in particular was able to position its lobster well…

image.caption: The lingering impacts of tariffs, as well as competition, are expected to be challenges during this year's lobster season. (Robert Short/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

The Canadian lobster industry is thinking of ways to recapture the Chinese market after competitors took advantage of retaliatory tariffs. Vietnam in particular was able to position its lobster well in 2025, filling the gap Canada left and becoming a strong competitor.
Retaliatory tariffs from China gave Canada’s competitors, such as Vietnam, the upper hand
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 16, 2026 5:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 2 hours ago

As the lobster industry in southwest Nova Scotia gears up for the beginning of its season at the end of the month, some are looking to the market in China — and wondering if Canadian lobster can once again take the lead.

China is Canada's second-largest market for seafood. But according to data from Statistics Canada shared with CBC, the value of lobster exports to China dropped from $521 million in 2024 to $314 million in 2025.

Kris Vascotto, executive director of the Nova Scotia Seafood Alliance, said the retaliatory Chinese tariff on Canadian seafood introduced in March 2025 is partially to blame. And while the tariff was suspended in March 2026 and will remain paused until 2028, he thinks it will be hard to undo the damage.
“As we got into 2026, even after the tariffs were removed and we're back in that same retail environment as we were in 2024, we had a really tough time trying to get momentum back,” he said.

Competitors like Vietnam and Australia filled the gap left by Canada in 2025. Vietnam in particular became the fastest-growing lobster competitor, thanks to high demand for its live green spiny lobster, which is multi-coloured and clawless.
Vascotto said the impact could have been even bigger if not for a flood in Vietnam that took out many of its lobster farms in November 2025.
“They've restocked their cages, they've rebuilt their cages stronger. Their production appears to be going up,” Vascotto said.
“So now we're in a position where we're looking forward to our larger fall season that's coming into play and we're understanding that there's going to be some real market challenges there.”

People stand near fishing vessels that were piled up in wrecks along the main road after being washed ashore by Typhoon Kalmaegi at Vung Cheo Fishing Village in central Vietnam, where hundreds of lobster farms had been washed away or damaged, in Xuan Cau District, Dak Lak province, Vietnam, Nov. 8, 2025. (Minh Nguyen/Reuters)

Geoff Irvine, the executive director of the Lobster Council of Canada, said Vietnamese lobster is mainly an aquaculture product, which means that unlike Canadian lobster, it is not caught by fishermen in the wild, but rather raised from larvae to adulthood.
That difference is one of the strengths the Canadian product has over the competition, he said, and the strategy to regain the Chinese market is to tell that to consumers.
“It's wild caught, it's from the cold waters of Canada. It's traceable and sustainable. So we have a great story to tell,” said Irvine.

He is hoping to secure some funding from the Atlantic Fisheries Fund to do additional marketing in China, including social media campaigns, collaborations with chefs and programs, and more direct trade missions.
Lobster boats, loaded with pots and buoys, head from West Dover, N.S., on Tuesday, Nov. 29, 2022, for the opening of the season in Lobster Fishing Area 33. (The Canadian Press)

In late October, Irvine went to Qingdao, China, for the world’s largest seafood expo. He was there alongside other Canadian industry representatives, as well as the federal and provincial fisheries ministers.
Irvine said he heard directly from Chinese importers and consumers and learned more about what they want from their Canadian partners.
Irvine also said he had the chance to meet some of the competitors.
“The Australian lobster industry is also very concerned about Vietnamese competition. And they've been on site in Vietnam. They've been at the [lobster] farms,” he said.
Dead lobsters are being collected at the shrimp farm of Cao Van Luu, 36, after floods swept through the area on Nov. 25, 2025, in Dak Lak province, Vietnam. (Thanh Hue/Getty Images)

After the event, Fisheries and Oceans Canada posted a news release highlighting the visit, including federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson meeting with seafood buyers and government representatives.

“These engagements showcased Canada's leadership in sustainable fisheries management and reinforced its reputation as a reliable supplier of safe, sustainably harvested, high-quality seafood,” read the release.
CBC reached out to Thompson, but she was not available for an interview.

Nova Scotia Fisheries Minister Kent Smith was also unavailable for an interview. His department sent a statement saying the trip “gave Nova Scotia companies direct access to buyers and a chance to hear what they need.”

“What we’ve heard from buyers in China is that the market is evolving. Consumers are looking for premium seafood that is convenient, nutritious, and sustainably sourced. That plays to Nova Scotia's strengths,” the department said in the statement.
Irvine believes the competition from Vietnam, as well as higher fuel prices that impact the cost of fishing, make for a difficult season ahead.

“Everybody hopes for the best and plans for the worst. That's the nature of the seafood sector,” he said. “We monitor prices and we monitor trends weekly, daily, and so does everybody in the sector. And I think it's well-accepted that we're coming into a very challenging period.”
For Vascotto, not all hope is lost. He said the removal of the tariffs did give the industry some relief, and the continued pause also gives importers more confidence in the Canadian lobster market.
“It's going to take time, but we do have the momentum behind us. We are beginning to see that uptick,” he said.
According to the province, from April through July 2026, Nova Scotia seafood exports to China were about 30 per cent higher than during the same period last year.

Vascotto said while efforts to get back on China's good side continue, some in the local industry are also looking to expand their markets, eyeing other parts of Asia and Europe to diversify and not depend on any one nation.
